parts.title: Hiring a venue for a party
parts.intro: You will hear a woman phoning a hotel to ask about hiring a room for a party.

script.t: Good morning, Riverside Hotel, events team. James speaking.
Hello. I’m organising a party for my parents’ fortieth wedding anniversary, and I wanted to ask about hiring one of your rooms.
Of course. When is the party?
It’s on Saturday the 21st of June.
script.say: It’s on Saturday the twenty-first of June.

script.t: Let me look. Yes, we have availability that evening. How many guests are you expecting?
We’ve invited about seventy people, but some of them won’t be able to come, so I’d say around sixty.
Then I’d suggest the Garden Room. The Terrace Room only holds fifty, and the Ballroom would feel very empty with sixty people.
The Garden Room sounds lovely.
It is. It opens onto the lawn, so if the weather’s good, guests can go outside. Now, the room hire is £350 for the evening, from seven until midnight.
script.say: It is. It opens onto the lawn, so if the weather’s good, guests can go outside. Now, the room hire is three hundred and fifty pounds for the evening, from seven until midnight.

script.t: Does that include food?
No, catering is separate. We have three menus. The cheapest is a cold buffet. Then there’s a hot buffet, and finally a three-course sit-down meal.
My parents aren’t keen on formal dinners, and the cold buffet might not be enough in the evening. I think we’ll go for the hot one.
Good choice. It’s our most popular. Is there anyone with special dietary needs?
Yes, my uncle can’t eat nuts, and there will be a few vegetarians.
That’s no problem. I’ll make a note about the nuts for the chef.
Now, can we bring our own music?
Yes, you can bring a band or a DJ. We just ask that the music stops by 11.30, because we have guests staying in the rooms upstairs.
script.say: Yes, you can bring a band or a DJ. We just ask that the music stops by half past eleven, because we have guests staying in the rooms upstairs.

script.t: Fine. And decorations? I’d like to put up some photos of my parents.
Certainly, but please don’t use tape on the walls; it damages the paint. We can provide boards for displaying photos.
That’s helpful. What about parking?
We have a car park with space for forty cars, and it’s free for party guests. You just need to give your name at reception.
Great. And to confirm the booking?
We ask for a deposit of 20%, which is £70, and the rest is paid two weeks before the event.
script.say: We ask for a deposit of twenty per cent, which is seventy pounds, and the rest is paid two weeks before the event.

script.t: And if we have to cancel?
The deposit is refunded if you cancel at least a month in advance.
OK. Could you email me the details? My address is k.marsh@quickmail.com. That’s Marsh, M, A, R, S, H.
script.say: OK. Could you email me the details? My address is k dot marsh at quickmail dot com. That’s Marsh, M, A, R, S, H.

script.t: I’ll send it this afternoon.

parts.title: A guide to a new library
parts.intro: You will hear a librarian talking to a group of visitors at a city’s new central library.

script.t: Hello everyone, and welcome to the new Central Library. I’m Sarah, and I’m going to tell you a bit about the building and what it offers before you explore on your own.

The library opened in March, replacing the old library on King Street, which had become far too small. The new building was designed by a local architect, and what makes it special is that it uses very little energy. The roof is covered with solar panels, and the building is heated using warmth from underground.
Since we opened, visitor numbers have been much higher than we expected. We thought most of our visitors would be students, but in fact the biggest group has been families with young children.

Membership is free for everyone who lives or works in the city. To join, you just need to show something with your address on it, such as a bill. You don’t need a photo, as we take one when you register.

You can borrow up to twelve items at a time, for three weeks. One change from the old library is that we no longer charge fines for late returns. We found that fines stopped people from coming back, which wasn’t what we wanted.
We also run lots of events. The most popular so far has been our weekly coding club for teenagers, which always has a waiting list.
Now, let me show you where things are on this plan of the ground floor. We’re standing at the main entrance, at the bottom of the plan.
Directly ahead of you is the information desk. If you need help, that’s the place to go.
On your right as you come in, just past the lockers, you’ll find the café. It’s a nice place to sit with a newspaper, and it looks out onto the street.
The children’s library is on the left-hand side of the building, at the far end. We put it there so that it’s away from the quiet study areas. You’ll see it has big windows overlooking the garden.
Next to the information desk, on its left, there’s a room with computers that you can use for free for up to two hours a day. That’s the computer room.
The local history room is in the far right-hand corner. It holds old maps and photographs of the city, and staff there can help you trace your family history.
And finally, the exhibition space is in the centre of the building, behind the information desk, under the glass roof. At the moment there’s a display of children’s book illustrations.
The stairs and lifts to the upper floors are next to the café. So, enjoy your visit.

parts.title: A field trip report
parts.intro: You will hear two geography students, Mia and Daniel, discussing a field trip report with their tutor.

script.t: Come in, both of you. So, you’re writing up the field trip to the river. How’s it going?
Pretty well. We’ve finished the introduction and the methods section. The results are taking longer than we expected, though.
Why is that?
Mostly because some of our measurements don’t make sense. At one of the sites, the water seemed to be flowing faster than further downstream, which is the opposite of what we predicted.
We think the equipment may not have been working properly at that site. The float we used kept getting caught in the plants.
That’s quite possible. Don’t hide it, though. Explain it in your report. Examiners like to see that you’ve thought about the limitations of your data.
OK. What about the photographs? We took loads.
Choose three or four that show something specific, and label them clearly. Don’t include pictures just because they look nice.
Right. And how long should the discussion be? We’ve written almost two thousand words.
That’s too long for this assignment. The whole report should be about three thousand, so I’d aim to cut the discussion by half.
That’s going to be hard. Daniel wants to keep the part about the history of the river.
I think it explains why the river is shaped the way it is.
It’s interesting, but it’s background. Put a short version in the introduction and focus the discussion on your own results.
And the deadline is still the fifteenth?
Actually, I’ve given everyone an extra week because of the problem with the minibus, so it’s now the twenty-second.
Now, let’s talk about what each of you thought of the trip. Mia, what did you find most useful?
Honestly, measuring the river ourselves. Reading about how rivers work is one thing, but actually standing in the water made it much easier to understand.
And Daniel?
Working as a team. Usually we work on our own, so I learned a lot about dividing up tasks and communicating.
That’s an important skill. Employers often say it’s one of the things graduates lack. Was there anything you’d change?
The timing. We only had one day at the river, and there wasn’t enough time to collect data at all eight sites. We had to skip two of them.
For me, it was the preparation. We should have practised using the equipment before the trip. We wasted the first hour working out how it all worked.
Those are fair points. I’ll pass them on to the department. And would you recommend the trip to next year’s students?
Definitely. Even with the problems, it was the best part of the course so far.
I agree.
Good. I look forward to reading the report.

parts.title: How cities can cool down
parts.intro: You will hear part of a lecture about the urban heat island effect.

script.t: Today I’d like to look at a problem that’s becoming more serious as the climate warms: the urban heat island effect. This is the name given to the fact that cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them.
The difference is greatest at night. During the day, buildings and roads absorb heat from the sun, and after sunset they slowly release it, so the city cools down much more slowly than rural areas.
There are several causes. The first is the materials cities are made from. Dark surfaces such as asphalt absorb much more heat than grass or soil.
In some large cities, the difference can be as much as ten degrees on a summer night. And it isn’t only big cities: even small towns show the effect to some extent.
Second, cities have fewer trees and plants. Plants cool the air through a process called evapotranspiration, in which water evaporates from their leaves. Without them, that natural cooling is lost.
Third, the shape of the city matters. Tall buildings close together trap heat and block the wind, which would otherwise carry warm air away.
And finally, there’s the heat produced by human activity itself: cars, factories and, ironically, air-conditioning units, which pump hot air out into the street.
Why does this matter? Above all, because of health. During heatwaves, death rates rise sharply in cities, and elderly people are particularly at risk.
Higher temperatures also increase the demand for electricity, as people use more air-conditioning, and this can put pressure on the power supply.

There are environmental costs too. Warm water running off hot pavements into rivers after a storm can harm fish, and higher temperatures speed up the chemical reactions that produce smog, so air quality gets worse.

So what can be done? One of the simplest solutions is to change the colour of surfaces. Painting roofs white reflects sunlight, and studies have shown that this can reduce the temperature inside a building by several degrees.
Another approach is green roofs, where plants are grown on top of buildings. As well as cooling, they absorb rainwater, which reduces the risk of flooding.
Planting trees along streets is also very effective. The shade they provide can make the surface of a pavement up to twenty degrees cooler.

Some cities are also bringing back water. In Seoul, a motorway was removed to uncover a stream that had been buried under concrete, and the area around it is now noticeably cooler than nearby streets.

Of course, these projects have to be planned carefully. Trees need space for their roots and regular watering while they are young, and some species produce pollen that causes problems for people with allergies. So choosing the right trees for the right streets is important.
None of these solutions is enough on its own, but together they can make a real difference. Next week, we’ll look at how some cities are measuring the effect street by street.
